text: We get a strong signal, then we can use large constellations because we get very clean signals and the error probability will be low. If instead the channel is bad, that means the received signal is weak and comes with interference other issues, then we have to be careful. We want to make sure that the receiver will be able to extract the bits correctly to understand what signal that is. And in order to do that, it will be better to use, for example, a binary modulation, where we have only two signals but they are very well distinguished. So even if the signal when traveling gets weaker and deteriorated, we're still able to say, okay, this signal that I received that is placed here is likely this one, and will be correct. Okay. So depending on channel conditions, we may use essentially more, let's say, robust modulations like the binary one, or more efficient modulations like this one with eight, not just two but eight signals, so that we are able to let each signal carry, for example, three bits, like in this case, instead of one, and increase our speed. Is that clear? Okay. Now that said, there are actually many different types of modulations.
